mainTopic: שומר שמסר לשומר, and the dispute about negligence followed by a natural death (marsh and cliff cases)
overview: The amud opens by finishing an answer for רבי יוחנן's view that a שומר who hands a deposit to someone else is liable. His own wife and children are an exception, because the owner expects them to be around. The sages of נהרדעא show that the wording of the משנה supports this. רבא rules as final הלכה that a שומר who hands a deposit to another שומר is always liable, because the owner trusts only the first שומר's oath. Next, אביי and רבא both quote רבה on a careless שומר whose animal wandered into a marsh and died naturally. אביי says he is liable because the marsh killed it, and רבא says he is exempt because death would have come anywhere. Each admits a limit to his view. Then each defends his view against a challenge, including a long back-and-forth about a משנה on animals at the cliffs. Finally, שמואל rules like רבי יוסי that a renter may not profit from the owner's cow, and רב שמואל בר יהודה begins to question how far that ruling reaches, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: An owner expects the guardian's family to be involved
steps.stepSummary: The end of an answer: a שומר's own wife and adult children are different from strangers, because the owner gives the deposit knowing they will be around it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He deposits it with the understanding that the guardian's wife and children will also be involved.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an answer it began before this section. Giving the deposit to one's own adult children is allowed, because the owner expected the family to be around it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן holds that a שומר who hands the deposit to someone else is liable. The משנה seems to free him when he gives it to his adult children. The answer is that family is a special case: no שומר can watch an item every minute, so the owner silently agrees that the household will help.

keyTerms.meaning: one who deposits an item with a guardian

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean any handing-over is fine. Only the guardian's own household is included, because the owner already expected it.

phrases.english: With the awareness of his wife and his children
he (the owner) deposits it.

steps.triggerLanguage: עַל דַּעַת אִשְׁתּוֹ וּבָנָיו הוּא מַפְקִיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a defense of רבי יוחנן against a challenge from the משנה, which began before this section.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: one's own family is different from outsiders
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the משנה frees a שומר who gave the deposit to his adult children, maybe handing a deposit to any responsible adult is fine.
steps.terutzMaskana: Family members are an exception, since the owner expected them to be involved. Handing the deposit to outsiders still makes the שומר liable.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Giving a deposit to one's own adult household members does not count as improperly handing it to someone else.

steps.title: The wording of the משנה supports the family distinction
steps.stepSummary: The sages of נהרדעא point out that the משנה specifically says 'his' minor children. That shows adult and minor outsiders are treated the same, and the adult-versus-minor difference exists only within one's own family.
steps.simpleTranslation: The sages of נהרדעא say: The wording is precise too. It teaches: 'Or if he handed them to his minor son or daughter, he is liable.' So if he gave them to his adult son or daughter, he is exempt. This shows that with other people, adults or minors make no difference: he is liable. Otherwise, the משנה should have just said 'minors' in general. Learn from this.
steps.whatsHappening: The sages of נהרדעא bring support for the answer in step 1 from the exact wording of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If adults and minors were treated differently for everyone, the משנה would have said simply 'minors.' Instead it said 'his son and daughter who are minors.' That extra detail tells us the adult-versus-minor difference matters only for one's own children. With outsiders, the שומר is liable either way.

keyTerms.meaning: the wording is also precise (it supports this)
let it teach in general, without adding details
learn from it; this proves it

steps.whatToRemember: With one's own children, only minors make the שומר liable. With outsiders, he is liable whether they are adults or minors.

phrases.english: The sages of Neharde'a say:
The wording is also precise, as it teaches:
phrases.notes: They are quoting a משנה later in this פרק, about a שומר who was given coins to guard.

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ שֶׁמְּסָרָן לִבְנוֹ וּבִתּוֹ הַקְּטַנִּים – חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: Or if he handed them to his minor son and daughter, he is liable.
But to his adult son and daughter, he is exempt.
It follows that regarding other people,

phrases.aramaic: לָא שְׁנָא גְּדוֹלִים וְלָא שְׁנָא קְטַנִּים – חַיָּיב,
phrases.english: it makes no difference whether adults or minors: he is liable,
for if so, it should have just said 'minors' in general.
phrases.notes: 'If so' means: if outsiders who are adults were also allowed.

phrases.english: Learn from this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the family distinction from step 1 using the exact wording of the משנה.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that only one's own family is an exception, while outsiders of any age make the שומר liable
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's extra words 'his son and daughter' instead of a general 'minors'

steps.title: רבא's final ruling: a guardian who hands off a deposit is liable
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules as הלכה that a שומר who gives the deposit to another שומר is liable. This is true even when he gives it to a שומר שכר, who carries more responsibility.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא says the הלכה is: A guardian who handed the deposit to another guardian is liable. It is obvious when a paid guardian hands it to an unpaid guardian, since he lowered the level of its protection. But even an unpaid guardian who hands it to a paid guardian is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא settles the argument in practice and rules like רבי יוחנן: handing a deposit to another guardian makes you liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The easy case is a שומר שכר handing it to a שומר חנם, because the new guardian takes less responsibility. The surprising part is that even a שומר חנם handing it to a שומר שכר is liable, though the item now seems to have more protection. That raises the obvious question of why, which comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: a guardian who handed the item to another guardian
a paid guardian (liable even for theft and loss)
an unpaid guardian (liable only for negligence)
it is obvious for this case, and it is true even in that case

steps.whatToRemember: The final הלכה: a שומר who hands a deposit to another שומר is liable, in either direction.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the practical ruling for the whole argument about a שומר who hands the deposit to someone else.

phrases.english: Rava says: The halakha is:
A guardian who handed it to another guardian is liable.

phrases.aramaic: לָא מִבַּעְיָא שׁוֹמֵר שָׂכָר שֶׁמָּסַר לְשׁוֹמֵר חִנָּם
phrases.english: It is not necessary to say this for a paid guardian who handed it to an unpaid guardian,
since he lowered its level of protection.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אֲפִילּוּ שׁוֹמֵר חִנָּם שֶׁמָּסַר לְשׁוֹמֵר שָׂכָר – חַיָּיב,
phrases.english: but even an unpaid guardian who handed it to a paid guardian is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא, הִלְכְתָא: שׁוֹמֵר שֶׁמָּסַר לְשׁוֹמֵר – חַיָּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the defense and support in steps 1 and 2, רבא gives the final practical ruling.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A שומר who hands a deposit to another שומר is liable, even if the second שומר carries more responsibility.

steps.title: Why is the unpaid guardian liable?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks why a שומר חנם who gave the item to a שומר שכר is liable, when the item now seems better protected.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא himself asks for the reason behind the surprising half of his ruling. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שומר שכר pays even for theft and loss, so the owner seems to have gained. The question is what harm the owner suffered that makes the first guardian liable.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the second half of רבא's ruling in step 3.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why a שומר חנם is liable for handing the deposit to a שומר שכר, who carries more responsibility

steps.title: The owner trusts only the original guardian's oath
steps.stepSummary: The owner can say: I trust your oath, but I do not trust the oath of the person you gave it to.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because the owner can say to him: You are someone I trust when you swear. That person is not someone I trust when he swears.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers, as part of his own statement, that the owner chose to rely on this particular guardian's honesty, and he does not have to accept someone else's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Any guardian can get out of paying in some cases by taking a שבועה about what happened. Even a שומר שכר still swears in some cases, such as an אונס. The owner trusted the first guardian's word under oath, not a stranger's, so handing the item over damages the owner's position.
steps.whatToRemember: The real issue is trust: the owner picked whose oath he relies on.

phrases.english: Because he (the owner) can say to him:
You are trusted by me with an oath,
that one is not trusted by me with an oath.

steps.triggerLanguage: דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ: אַתְּ מְהֵימְנַתְּ לִי בִּשְׁבוּעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The owner trusts only the original guardian's oath, so handing the item to anyone else is a loss to him.

steps.title: Negligence followed by natural death: a dispute in רבה's name
steps.stepSummary: A new topic: a guardian was negligent and the animal wandered into a marsh, but it died naturally. אביי quotes רבה saying he is liable. רבא quotes רבה saying he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: If he was negligent with it, and it went out to a marsh, and it died in its normal way: אביי, in the name of רבה, says he is liable. רבא, in the name of רבה, says he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new discussion with a dispute. A guardian was careless, but the animal died of natural causes, not from the danger his carelessness created.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The guardian did something wrong by letting the animal reach a dangerous marsh, but it was not stolen or eaten there. אביי's version of רבה holds him liable, and step 7 explains that the marsh itself is blamed for the death. רבא's version exempts him, and step 8 explains that a natural death would have come anywhere. Both students quote the same teacher, so the argument is also about what רבה really said.

keyTerms.meaning: it was stated (introduces an argument between אמוראים)
a marsh (a dangerous place with thieves and wild animals)
it died in its normal way (natural death)

steps.confusionAlert: Both אביי and רבא are quoting the same teacher, רבה. They disagree about what רבה ruled, not only with each other.

phrases.english: It was stated:
He was negligent with it, and it went out to a marsh,
and it died in its normal way.
Abaye, in the name of Rabba, says: He is liable.
Rava, in the name of Rabba, says: He is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִתְּמַר: פָּשַׁע בָּהּ וְיָצָאת לַאֲגַם, וּמֵתָה כְּדַרְכָּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new discussion about negligence followed by an אונס, after the topic of handing a deposit to another guardian is settled.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There are two versions of רבה's ruling on negligence followed by natural death: liable (אביי) or exempt (רבא).

steps.title: אביי's version: the guardian is liable because the marsh killed it
steps.stepSummary: אביי, quoting רבה, says the שומר is liable. This is true even for those who usually exempt a case of תחילתו בפשיעה וסופו באונס, because the marsh air is what killed the animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said in the name of רבה: he is liable. Any judge who does not rule this way is not a real judge. Those who say a case that starts with negligence and ends with an accident is liable would obviously make him liable. But even those who say such a case is exempt would make him liable here. Why? Because we say the marsh air killed it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now explains אביי's side of the dispute from Step 6. He gives his ruling and the reason behind it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a known dispute about a case that starts with negligence and ends in an accident. אביי says that dispute does not matter here, because this death is not really an accident. The negligence led the animal into the marsh, and the marsh air caused the death, so the negligence is the real cause.

keyTerms.meaning: Starting with negligence and ending with an accident beyond one's control

steps.confusionAlert: אביי is not taking a side in the general dispute about negligence followed by an accident. He is saying that this case is different, because here the negligence itself caused the death.

phrases.english: Abaye said in the name of Rabba: he is liable,
any judge who does not rule

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הַאי דִּינָא לָאו דַּיָּינָא הוּא.
phrases.english: according to this law is not a judge.
It is not necessary to say, according to the one who says
that a case starting with negligence and ending by accident
is liable, that he is liable.
But even according to the one who says such a case is exempt,
here he is liable.
What is the reason? Because we say:
the air of the marsh killed it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands אביי's half of the dispute introduced in Step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The שומר is liable even for those who usually exempt a case of negligence followed by an accident, because the marsh air killed the animal.

steps.title: רבא's version: the guardian is exempt because death comes anywhere
steps.stepSummary: רבא, quoting רבה, says the שומר is exempt. This is true even for those who usually make תחילתו בפשיעה וסופו באונס liable, because a natural death would have happened in any place.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said in the name of רבה: he is exempt. Any judge who does not rule this way is not a real judge. Those who say a case that starts with negligence and ends with an accident is exempt would obviously exempt him. But even those who say such a case is liable would exempt him here. Why? Because we say about the Angel of Death: what difference does it make whether here or there?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now explains רבא's opposite version of רבה's ruling, using the same structure as אביי's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא sees the death as completely natural. The animal would have died in the same way at home, so the negligence did not cause the loss. That is why even those who usually make negligence followed by an accident liable would exempt the שומר here.

keyTerms.meaning: Exempt; he does not have to pay
The Angel of Death; here it stands for a natural death

keyTerms.term: מָה לִי הָכָא וּמָה לִי הָתָם
keyTerms.meaning: What difference does it make to me whether here or there?

steps.whyThisMatters: אביי and רבא are arguing about how to view the death. Was it caused by the place (the marsh), or would it have happened no matter where the animal was?

phrases.english: Rava said in the name of Rabba: he is exempt,
any judge who does not rule

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הַאי דִּינָא לָאו דַּיָּינָא הוּא.
phrases.english: according to this law is not a judge.
It is not necessary to say, according to the one who says
that a case starting with negligence and ending by accident
is exempt, that he is exempt.
But even according to the one who says such a case is liable,
here he is exempt.
What is the reason? Because we say:
the Angel of Death:

phrases.aramaic: מָה לִי הָכָא וּמָה לִי הָתָם.
phrases.english: what is the difference to me whether here, and what is the difference to me whether there?
phrases.notes: He means that a natural death would have reached the animal wherever it was, so the marsh changed nothing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite version, built exactly like אביי's in Step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The שומר is exempt even for those who usually make negligence followed by an accident liable, because a natural death would have happened anywhere.

steps.title: אביי agrees: if the animal came home and died, the guardian is exempt
steps.stepSummary: אביי admits that if the animal returned from the marsh to its owner's house and died there, the שומר is exempt, because we can no longer say the marsh killed it.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי agrees that if the animal went back to its owner's house and died there, he is exempt. Why? Because it came back, so we cannot say the marsh air killed it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows where אביי's reasoning stops. He agrees to a case where the guardian goes free.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי's whole reason was that the marsh air killed the animal. Once the animal made it back home safely, that reason no longer fits. So even אביי exempts the guardian.

phrases.english: And Abaye agrees
that if it returned to its owner's house
and died, that he is exempt.
What is the reason? Because it returned,
and one cannot say
that the air of the marsh killed it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets a limit on אביי's ruling from Step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the animal returned home and died there, even אביי exempts the guardian.

steps.title: רבא agrees: if a thief took it from the marsh, the guardian is liable
steps.stepSummary: רבא admits that if a thief stole the animal from the marsh and it died naturally in the thief's house, the שומר is liable, because even without the death the animal would have been lost to the thief.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא agrees that any time a thief stole the animal in the marsh and it died a natural death in the thief's house, he is liable. Why? Because even if the Angel of Death had spared it, it would be standing in the thief's house.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows where רבא's reasoning stops. He agrees to a case where the guardian must pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's reason was that the death would have come anyway, so the negligence caused no loss. When a thief takes the animal, the owner loses it to the theft even if it never dies. That loss came from the negligence, so the guardian pays.

keyTerms.meaning: In its normal way; a natural death

steps.whatToRemember: אביי: liable because the marsh killed it, but exempt if it came home and died. רבא: exempt because death comes anywhere, but liable if a thief took it from the marsh.

phrases.english: And Rava agrees that any time
that if a thief stole it in the marsh
and it died in its normal way in the thief's house, that he is liable.
What is the reason?
Because if the Angel of Death had spared it,
it would be standing in the thief's house.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets a limit on רבא's ruling from Step 8, matching אביי's admission in Step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If a thief stole the animal from the marsh and it died naturally in his house, even רבא makes the guardian liable.

steps.title: אביי challenges רבא from the exchange of רבי אבא בר ממל and רבי אמי
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks רבא: if 'what difference does it make whether here or there' is a valid reason, why didn't רבי אמי use it to answer רבי אבא בר ממל's objection? Instead, he answered that the owner had given permission to lend.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to רבא: according to you, who say about the Angel of Death 'what difference does it make whether here or there,' look at the objection רבי אבא בר ממל raised against רבי אמי. רבי אמי answered that the owner had given permission to lend. Why didn't he just say: the Angel of Death, what difference does it make whether here or there!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי attacks רבא's reasoning by pointing to an earlier discussion in which that reasoning would have been the easy answer, yet nobody used it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the earlier case, a renter lent the cow to someone else, and it died naturally. רבי אמי explained the exemption with a special case: the owner had allowed lending. If רבא's logic were correct, רבי אמי could have simply said the natural death would have happened with either person. Since he did not say that, it seems the reasoning is not accepted.

keyTerms.meaning: He raised an objection against him
Let him say to him (why didn't he say?)

phrases.english: Abaye said to Rava: according to you,
who said about the Angel of Death:

phrases.aramaic: מָה לִי הָכָא וּמָה לִי הָתָם,
phrases.english: what is the difference to me whether here, and what is the difference to me whether there,

phrases.aramaic: הַאי דְּאוֹתְבֵיהּ רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר מֶמֶל לְרַבִּי אַמֵּי
phrases.english: that objection which Rabbi Abba bar Memel raised against Rabbi Ami,
phrases.notes: This is the earlier discussion about a renter who lent the cow to someone else, after which it died a natural death.

phrases.english: and he answered him
that it is a case where the owner gave him permission to lend,
but let him say to him:

phrases.aramaic: מַלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת מָה לִי הָכָא וּמָה לִי הָתָם!
phrases.english: the Angel of Death, what is the difference to me whether here and what is the difference to me whether there!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reasoning רבא gave in Step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's principle that a natural death makes the location irrelevant (מלאך המות מה לי הכא ומה לי התם).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the principle were valid, רבי אמי would have used it as the simple answer to רבי אבא בר ממל. He gave a narrower answer, the owner's permission to lend, instead.

steps.title: רבא: The objection depends on אביי's reason, not mine
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the objection of רבי אבא בר ממל only arises under אביי's reason for why transferring a deposit is wrong ("I don't want my deposit in another's hand"). Under רבא's reason ("I trust your oath, not his"), there is no objection at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to אביי: According to you, who teach that the owner can say "I don't want my deposit in someone else's hand," there is room to raise that objection. But according to me, who says the owner can say "I trust your oath, but I don't trust that other person's oath," there is no objection at all.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא defends himself against אביי's question from step 11. He shows that the earlier objection only fits אביי's way of explaining the law, not his own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Why is a שומר not allowed to hand a deposit to another שומר? אביי holds that the owner can say 'I don't want my deposit in someone else's hand.' רבא holds the reason he gave in step 5: the owner doesn't trust the second שומר's oath. רבי אבא בר ממל's objection only makes sense under אביי's reason, so רבי אמי's answer proves nothing against רבא.

keyTerms.meaning: An item left with a שומר for safekeeping
An oath (here, the oath a שומר takes to be cleared)
To raise an objection against it

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two reasons. אביי says the owner simply doesn't want his item with a stranger. רבא says the owner doesn't trust the stranger's oath. The whole answer depends on which reason you hold.

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: רבא is answering אביי's question from the previous step.

phrases.english: According to you, who teach
"I don't want my deposit to be in someone else's hand"
there is room to raise that objection;
but according to me, since I say:
"You are trusted by me with an oath,
and that other one is not trusted by me with an oath"
there is no room to raise the objection at all.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's challenge from step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The objection depends on the other side's reasoning
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי אמי's not using 'what difference does it make' shows that רבא's reasoning is wrong.
steps.terutzMaskana: That objection only exists under אביי's reason for the transfer rule. Under רבא's reason, it never arises.

steps.title: רמי בר חמא challenges אביי from the cliff case
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא quotes a משנה. If a שומר took the animal up to the cliffs and it fell, he is liable. This implies that if it died naturally there, it is an אונס and he is exempt. But by אביי's logic, the owner should be able to say the mountain air or the strain of the climb killed it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא objected: "If he brought the animal up to the tops of the cliffs and it fell, that is not an accident, and he is liable." This implies that if it died a natural death there, it is an accident and he is exempt. But why? Let the owner say: the mountain air killed it, or the strain of the mountain killed it!
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר חמא brings a משנה that seems to go against אביי. In that משנה, an animal taken to a risky place died naturally, and the שומר is exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי said the שומר is liable for a natural death in the marsh, because the marsh air killed the animal. Here the case is the same kind: the cliffs are a risky place, just like the marsh. Yet the משנה implies the שומר is exempt for a natural death there. So the 'the place killed it' argument seems to be rejected.

keyTerms.meaning: Raises an objection (usually from a משנה or ברייתא)
An accident beyond the שומר's control

phrases.english: Rami bar Chama objected:
If he brought it up to the tops of the cliffs and it fell,
this is not an accident, and he is liable.
This implies: if it died a natural death,
it is an accident and he is exempt.
But why? Let the owner say to him:
"The mountain air killed it,"
or else, "The strain of the mountain killed it!"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new challenge, this time against אביי's view.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's ruling in step 7 that the שומר is liable because the place killed the animal
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה implies a שומר is exempt for a natural death at the cliffs. That ignores the 'the place killed it' argument which אביי relies on.

steps.title: The משנה speaks of a good pasture
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה is talking about a שומר who took the animal to a rich, good pasture up there. Taking it there was not negligent in the first place.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are we dealing with here? A case where he brought it up to a rich, good pasture.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends אביי. It narrows the משנה to a case where going up the mountain was a normal, proper thing to do.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי's rule only applies when the שומר did something wrong at the start (תחילתו בפשיעה). If the cliffs held a good pasture where shepherds normally graze, bringing the animal there was not negligent. So there is no reason to blame the place.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (narrowing a source to a specific case)

phrases.english: What are we dealing with here?
Where he brought it up to a rich, good pasture.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רמי בר חמא's challenge.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה is talking about a שומר who wrongly took the animal to a dangerous place.
steps.terutzMaskana: Going up was proper because the pasture there was good, so there was no פשיעה at the start.

steps.title: Then he should be exempt even if it fell
steps.stepSummary: If taking the animal up was proper, why is the שומר liable when it falls?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, then even if it fell, he should be exempt!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer it just gave. If going up was fine, the משנה's ruling that he is liable for a fall no longer makes sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says a fall is not an אונס. But once we say the trip up was not negligent, a fall looks like an accident too. So the new reading seems to break the first half of the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: If so (if your answer is right)

phrases.english: If so, even if it fell, he should also be exempt!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: The good-pasture reading of the משנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If taking the animal up was not negligent, a fall should also count as an אונס. Yet the משנה makes him liable.

steps.title: He should have held the animal back
steps.stepSummary: For the fall he is liable for a different reason: he should have held onto the animal, and he didn't.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because he should have held it firmly, and he did not hold it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the שומר is still liable for a fall. His fault is not in going up but in failing to control the animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The negligence in a fall is a new one. A careful שומר grips the animal near a cliff edge, so a fall points to his own carelessness. A natural death has nothing to do with gripping, so for that he stays exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: To hold it firmly, to control it

phrases.english: Because he should have held it firmly, and he did not hold it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Pointing to a different act of negligence
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If going up was fine, nothing the שומר did is to blame for the fall.
steps.terutzMaskana: He is to blame for the fall because he failed to hold the animal back.

steps.title: But the first clause exempts him when it climbed and fell
steps.stepSummary: The first clause of the משנה says: if the animal climbed the cliffs on its own and fell, it is an אונס. But by the last answer, he should have held it back there too.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, look at the first clause: "If it climbed up to the tops of the cliffs and fell, this is an accident." But he should have held it back!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the 'he should have held it' answer, using the first clause of the same משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a שומר is always expected to hold the animal near a cliff, the first clause seems wrong. There the animal climbed and fell, and the משנה exempts him. The duty to hold the animal should make him liable there too.

keyTerms.meaning: He should have, he was required to

phrases.english: If so, look at the first clause:
"If it climbed up to the tops of the cliffs and fell,"
"this is an accident."
But he should have held it back!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 16 using the first clause of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a שומר is always required to hold the animal
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The first clause exempts him when the animal climbed and fell. If he had to hold it, he should be liable there.

steps.title: The animal overpowered him
steps.stepSummary: The first clause is talking about a case where the שומר tried to hold the animal, but it overpowered him going up and overpowered him coming down. So it really was an אונס.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the first clause is needed for a case where it overpowered him and went up, and overpowered him and came down.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the last challenge. It narrows the first clause to a case where the שומר did try to hold the animal, but failed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The duty to hold the animal still stands. In the first clause the שומר did his duty, but the animal was too strong for him, so the fall was a true accident. This keeps the whole משנה working with אביי's view.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for (this specific case)

steps.whatToRemember: The cliff משנה does not disprove אביי. Taking the animal to a good pasture is not negligent, so a natural death there is an אונס. A fall makes the שומר liable unless the animal overpowered him.

phrases.english: No, it is needed only
where it overpowered him and went up,
and overpowered him and came down.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 17.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: In the first clause the שומר could have held the animal and didn't.
steps.terutzMaskana: He tried, but the animal overpowered him, so it was a true אונס.

steps.title: Quoting רבי יוסי and ruling that the הלכה follows him
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי יוסי's words from the משנה, and רב יהודה reports in the name of שמואל that the הלכה follows רבי יוסי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי said: How can that person do business with his friend's cow, etc.? רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: The הלכה follows רבי יוסי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic by quoting רבי יוסי's line from the משנה. Then it brings שמואל's ruling that we follow רבי יוסי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, the שוכר lent the cow to a שואל, who has to pay. The תנא קמא says the שואל pays the שוכר. רבי יוסי objects that the שוכר would be making money off the owner's cow, so the payment should go back to the owner. שמואל rules like רבי יוסי.

keyTerms.meaning: The final law follows this opinion
Short for 'etc.', meaning the quote continues in the source

steps.whyThisMatters: This ruling decides who gets the payment when a rented animal is lent out and dies: the owner, not the middleman שוכר.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei said:
How can that one do business
phrases.notes: 'That one' is the renter, who lent the cow out to someone else.

phrases.english: with his cow, etc.
phrases.notes: 'His cow' means the owner's cow. The 'etc.' points to the rest of רבי יוסי's words in the משנה: the payment goes back to the owner.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
The halacha follows Rabbi Yosei.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי: כֵּיצַד הַלָּה עוֹשֶׂה סְחוֹרָה בְּפָרָתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the discussion of the animal on the cliffs and moves to a new section of the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שמואל rules that the הלכה follows רבי יוסי: the renter may not profit from the owner's cow, so the payment goes to the owner.

steps.title: רב שמואל בר יהודה recalls what רב יהודה said earlier
steps.stepSummary: רב שמואל בר יהודה reminds רב יהודה of something he once taught in שמואל's name about רבי יוסי's disagreement. His sentence continues in the next part.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שמואל בר יהודה said to רב יהודה: You told us in the name of שמואל: רבי יוסי was disagreeing...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. רב שמואל בר יהודה starts quoting an earlier teaching from שמואל to clarify how far רבי יוסי disagrees. The sentence is finished on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'the הלכה follows רבי יוסי' only tells us something if we know exactly where he argues. רב שמואל בר יהודה brings up an earlier report from שמואל about the scope of the argument. This sets up a clarification of what רב יהודה's ruling covers.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר יְהוּדָה לְרַב יְהוּדָה:
phrases.english: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda said to Rav Yehuda:
You told us in Shmuel's name:
Rabbi Yosei was disagreeing

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר יְהוּדָה לְרַב יְהוּדָה: אֲמַרְתְּ לַן מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins clarifying the reach of the ruling in step 19 by recalling an earlier statement from שמואל
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How far רבי יוסי's disagreement reaches, so we know what the ruling 'הלכה כרבי יוסי' covers. The question is completed in the next part.
